title: Go Goroutines: Scheduler, Stacks, and Leaks
summary: A deep field guide to Go's concurrency runtime: what a goroutine actually is, how the M:N scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads, how stacks start tiny and grow by copying, and how goroutines leak in production and how to find them.

chapters.title: What a Goroutine Actually Is
points: Definition: a goroutine is a function executing concurrently, managed by the Go runtime — not by the OS kernel
`go f(x)` starts one: the statement returns immediately, the call runs on a new goroutine, and the return value of `f` is discarded
A goroutine is the runtime struct `g` (in runtime/runtime2.go): stack bounds, program counter, status, scheduling links — roughly a few hundred bytes of bookkeeping
Initial stack is 2 KB (`_StackMin = 2048`); an OS thread reserves 1–8 MB of virtual memory by default, so goroutines are ~1000x cheaper to start
Cost comparison: goroutine creation ~1–2 µs and a switch ~tens of nanoseconds; an OS thread creation is ~10–100 µs and a kernel context switch ~1–2 µs
Goroutines are userspace-scheduled: a switch is a function call that swaps a few registers, never a `syscall` and never a kernel mode transition

Goroutine states you will see in traces: `_Grunnable` (queued), `_Grunning` (on a thread), `_Gsyscall` (in a syscall), `_Gwaiting` (parked on channel/mutex/timer), `_Gdead` (finished, on the free list)
Finished goroutine `g` structs go on a per-P free list (`gFree`) and are recycled, so steady-state churn allocates almost nothing
The `main` function runs on a goroutine; when `main` returns, the process exits and every other goroutine is killed mid-flight with no cleanup or defers
There is deliberately no goroutine ID in the public API — no goroutine-local storage, which forces explicit `context.Context` passing
Goroutines are not preallocated or pooled by the user: `sync.Pool` pools objects, not goroutines; spawning per-request is idiomatic
Example: `for i := range 3 { go func() { fmt.Println(i) }() }` is safe in Go 1.22+ because the loop variable is per-iteration; pre-1.22 all three printed 3
Concurrency is not parallelism: goroutines express independent work; `GOMAXPROCS` decides how much of it runs at literally the same instant
Gotcha: nothing waits for a goroutine implicitly — you need `sync.WaitGroup`, a channel, or `errgroup` or the work silently vanishes at exit

chapters.title: The M:N Model — G, M, and P
points: M:N means M goroutines are multiplexed onto N OS threads; the runtime, not the kernel, decides the mapping
`G` = goroutine (the work). `M` = machine, an OS thread (the worker). `P` = processor, the scheduling context and resource permit (the right to run Go code)
Hard rule: an M must hold a P to execute Go code. No P means the M parks or spins
`len(allp) == GOMAXPROCS`, fixed at startup and changeable with `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(n)` — it is the parallelism knob, not a thread limit
`GOMAXPROCS` defaults to `runtime.NumCPU()` since Go 1.5; Go 1.25 made it cgroup-aware so containers with a CPU quota no longer over-provision Ps
Thread count is separate and elastic: `runtime.SetMaxThreads` defaults to 10,000, and exceeding it is a fatal error, not a block
Why P exists at all: it owns the local run queue and the per-P mcache allocator, giving lock-free fast paths; the pre-1.1 scheduler had one global lock and did not scale
Each P owns a local run queue: a 256-slot lock-free ring plus a single `runnext` slot for the most recently readied goroutine
`runnext` is a latency optimization: a goroutine you just woke (for example a channel receiver) runs next, exploiting cache warmth, and inherits the remainder of the time slice
There is one global run queue (`sched.runq`) as the overflow and fairness backstop, guarded by the global scheduler lock
When a local queue overflows, the P moves half its goroutines (128) plus the new one to the global queue in one batch
`g0` is a special per-M goroutine that runs scheduler and runtime code on the system stack with a fixed, non-growable stack
Handoff: if an M blocks in a syscall, its P is detached and handed to another M so the other goroutines keep running
Diagram to memorize: many G circles, N P boxes each holding a queue, M threads docking into P boxes — Ms come and go, Ps stay put

chapters.title: Inside schedule(): Finding Work
points: The core loop is `schedule()`: find a runnable G, then `execute()` it; every scheduling decision funnels through here
Lookup order in `findRunnable()`: `runnext` slot, then local run queue, then global run queue, then the netpoller, then steal from other Ps
Fairness tick: every 61st schedule (`schedtick%61 == 0`) the P checks the global queue first, so global goroutines cannot be starved by a busy local queue
Work stealing: a P with nothing to do picks victims in random order over 4 passes and takes half of the victim's local queue
The last steal pass also takes the victim's `runnext`, but only after a brief spin, to avoid stealing a goroutine that is about to be run
Spinning Ms: a small number of threads spin looking for work before sleeping, so newly readied goroutines do not wait for a thread wake-up (~tens of µs saved)
The invariant guarding wake-ups: whenever work is submitted while an idle P exists, `wakep()` must run — missing that is how a runtime hang bug looks
Global scheduler lock is only taken for global queue access, idle P lists, and thread parking — the hot path is lock-free
`gopark()` moves the running G to `_Gwaiting`, unlinks it from the M, and returns to `schedule()`; `goready()` puts it back on a run queue
Channels, mutexes, `WaitGroup`, timers, and network I/O are all implemented on top of `gopark`/`goready` — one parking mechanism, many APIs
Blocked goroutines cost nothing: they hold no thread and are not polled — they sit on the wait queue of whatever they blocked on
The runtime deadlock detector only fires when every goroutine is asleep: `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` — it never catches a partial deadlock
`GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` prints a scheduler line every second: `runqueue=` (global), per-P queue lengths, `idleprocs`, `threads`, `spinningthreads`
`GODEBUG=scheddetail=1` adds a line per G, M, and P — verbose, but the direct way to see which goroutines are stuck and where

chapters.title: Preemption, Syscalls, and the Netpoller
points: `sysmon` is a monitor thread that runs without a P, sleeping 20 µs to 10 ms, and does retaking, preemption, netpoll, and forced GC
Time slice: a goroutine running longer than 10 ms is flagged for preemption by `sysmon`
Cooperative preemption (all versions): the function prologue compares SP against `stackguard0`; the runtime sets it to `stackPreempt` to force a yield at the next call
Cooperative preemption's fatal gap: a tight loop with no function calls and no allocation could never yield — one such loop could hang a stop-the-world GC forever
Async preemption (Go 1.14+): the runtime sends `SIGURG` to the thread and the handler pushes a call to `asyncPreempt`, so even `for {}` yields
Async preemption needs precise register maps at every instruction, which is why it required a compiler change, not just a runtime one
Blocking syscall path: `entersyscall` marks the P as `_Psyscall`; if the syscall returns fast, the M reacquires the same P and nothing else happens
If a syscall runs long, `sysmon` retakes the P (`retake`) and hands it to another M, so a blocked thread never idles a core
On return from a long syscall the goroutine has no P: it grabs an idle one or goes on the global run queue — this is why syscall-heavy code sees latency jitter
The netpoller wraps epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD/macOS), and IOCP (Windows): network reads and writes park the goroutine instead of blocking the thread
This is why blocking-looking code (`conn.Read(buf)`) scales to 100k connections — it is async I/O underneath with a synchronous API
Regular file I/O on Linux is not pollable, so it genuinely blocks an M; heavy disk workloads therefore inflate the thread count
cgo calls behave like syscalls: they occupy an M for their whole duration, so a slow C call costs a thread and can starve you of them
`runtime.LockOSThread()` pins a goroutine to its M for OS thread-local state (OpenGL contexts, Linux namespaces, some UI toolkits); always pair it with `UnlockOSThread` in a `defer`

chapters.title: Stacks That Grow
points: Every goroutine gets its own contiguous, heap-allocated stack starting at 2 KB — no `pthread` 8 MB reservation, so a million goroutines fits in a few GB
The compiler inserts a stack-bounds check in the prologue of any function that needs more than a tiny frame
On overflow the prologue calls `morestack`, which calls `newstack`: allocate a bigger stack, copy the old one over, fix up pointers, resume
Growth policy: double the size each time (2 KB, 4 KB, 8 KB …) so growth is amortized O(1) per byte
Copying is only safe because Go has precise stack maps: the GC knows every pointer slot in every frame, so pointers into the old stack can be rewritten

Pre-1.3 Go used segmented (split) stacks — a linked list of chunks — which had the hot-split problem: a call at a chunk boundary in a loop allocated and freed a segment every iteration, tanking performance
Go 1.3 replaced segments with copying stacks and Go 1.4 dropped the initial size from 8 KB to 2 KB
Stacks also shrink: at GC, if a goroutine uses less than 1/4 of its stack, the runtime halves it — long-lived goroutines that spiked once do not keep the memory
Hard limit: 1 GB per goroutine on 64-bit, 250 MB on 32-bit; adjustable via `debug.SetMaxStack`
Blowing the limit is fatal, not recoverable: `runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit` followed by `fatal error: stack overflow`
Infinite recursion therefore kills the whole process — `recover()` cannot catch a stack overflow
Stack memory is not counted by `HeapAlloc`; look at `MemStats.StackInuse` and `StackSys`, or the `goroutine` and `heap` pprof profiles together
Escape analysis interacts directly with this: values that outlive the frame move to the heap, keeping stacks small — check with `go build -gcflags='-m'`
Practical implication: deep recursive parsers and large stack arrays cause repeated copy-and-grow; hoisting a big buffer to the heap or reusing it removes the churn
`g0` (the scheduler stack) is exempt from growth — runtime code that runs on it must have bounded frames, which is why `//go:nosplit` exists

chapters.title: Channels, sync, and Parking
points: A channel is `hchan`: a ring buffer, an element size and count, a lock, and two wait queues (`sendq`, `recvq`) of `sudog` records
A `sudog` is the pairing of a parked goroutine with the value it is trying to send or receive — one goroutine can be on several wait queues (that is how `select` works)
Unbuffered send is a rendezvous: the sender parks until a receiver arrives, then the value is copied sender-to-receiver directly, skipping the buffer
Direct handoff optimization: on an unbuffered channel, the sender copies straight into the receiver's stack slot and calls `goready` — no intermediate copy
A send on a full buffered channel parks the sender on `sendq`; a receive drains the buffer, then moves a parked sender's value in
`close(ch)` readies every goroutine on both wait queues at once; receivers get the zero value with `ok == false`
Panic rules to memorize: send on closed channel panics, close of closed channel panics, close of nil channel panics; receive from closed channel is fine and never blocks
Nil channel operations block forever — deliberately useful in `select` to disable a case by setting its channel to nil
`select` with multiple ready cases picks uniformly at random, preventing systematic starvation of one case
`select` with a `default` never parks — that is how you write a non-blocking send or receive
`sync.Mutex` has a fast path (one atomic CAS, no runtime involvement) and a slow path that parks on a runtime semaphore
Mutex starvation mode: a goroutine waiting over 1 ms switches the mutex to FIFO handoff, trading throughput for bounded tail latency
`sync.WaitGroup` parks `Wait()` callers on a semaphore; `Add` must happen before the `go` statement or `Wait` can return early
`time.After` allocates a timer that is not collected until it fires — inside a hot `select` loop that is a real leak; use `time.NewTimer` and `Stop`, or `context.WithTimeout`
Channels are not free: expect ~100 ns per uncontended operation, so a mutex or atomic is often the right call for a shared counter

chapters.title: Patterns That Hold Up in Production
points: Worker pool: `N` goroutines ranging over one jobs channel, results on a second channel — bounds concurrency with no extra machinery
Semaphore pattern: a buffered channel of size N, acquire with `sem <- struct{}{}` and release with `defer func(){ <-sem }()`, when you want unbounded goroutines but bounded parallelism
Fan-out/fan-in: split work to many goroutines, merge with a `sync.WaitGroup` closing the merged output channel in its own goroutine
Pipeline stages: each stage takes an input channel, returns an output channel, and closes it when done — closure flows downstream and terminates the whole chain
`golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` is the default answer for parallel calls: it propagates the first error, cancels the shared context, and `Wait` collects everyone
`errgroup.SetLimit(n)` bounds concurrency inside the group, replacing hand-rolled semaphores
Ownership rule: the sender closes the channel, never the receiver — closing from the receive side races with in-flight sends and panics
Never write `go` in a library API where the caller cannot stop it; return a function or take a `context.Context` so shutdown is the caller's decision
Always pass `context.Context` as the first parameter and select on `ctx.Done()` in every loop that can block
`defer cancel()` after every `context.WithCancel`/`WithTimeout` — skipping it leaks the context's internal timer and goroutine until the parent dies
`sync.Once` for lazy singletons; `errgroup` or `WaitGroup` for joins; a `done chan struct{}` for broadcast shutdown (closing broadcasts to all receivers at once)
`runtime.Gosched()` yields voluntarily — almost never needed since async preemption, and its presence in code is usually a sign of a hidden bug
Rate limiting: `time.Ticker` plus a worker pool, or `golang.org/x/time/rate` — and always `defer ticker.Stop()`
Graceful shutdown: close the input channel, `Wait` for workers, then close outputs; a hard `os.Exit` skips every deferred cleanup in every goroutine

chapters.title: How Goroutines Leak
points: Definition of a leak: a goroutine that is permanently `_Gwaiting` or looping and is unreachable by any code that could finish it — the GC cannot collect a goroutine, only unreachable memory
Leaked goroutines hold their stack, their captured variables, and everything those reference, so a goroutine leak is also a memory leak
Cause 1 — send with no receiver: `ch <- v` on an unbuffered channel whose reader returned early on an error path; the classic HTTP-handler-with-timeout leak
Cause 2 — receive on a channel nobody closes: `for v := range ch` when the producer died from a panic or an early return
Cause 3 — `select` without a `ctx.Done()` or `done` case: the goroutine blocks forever once its only sender disappears
Cause 4 — forgetting `defer cancel()`: the context and its timer goroutine live until the parent context is cancelled, which for a background context is never
Cause 5 — `time.Ticker` without `Stop()`: the runtime timer keeps firing into a channel nobody drains
Cause 6 — `sync.WaitGroup` mismatch: a missing `Done()` (or a `Done()` skipped by an early `return` before the `defer`) blocks `Wait()` permanently
Cause 7 — unclosed `http.Response.Body`: the connection is never returned to the pool and the reader goroutine stays alive; `defer resp.Body.Close()` always, even when you ignore the body
Cause 8 — a worker pool whose jobs channel is never closed: `range` over it blocks forever after the last job
Cause 9 — mutual blocking under partial deadlock: two goroutines waiting on each other while the rest of the program runs fine, so the runtime deadlock detector stays silent
The fix for the unbuffered-send leak: give the result channel capacity 1 (`make(chan T, 1)`) so the sender can always complete and exit even if nobody reads
The general fix: every blocking operation gets an escape hatch — a `select` with `ctx.Done()`, a timeout, or a buffered channel sized for the worst case
Symptom profile: `runtime.NumGoroutine()` growing monotonically, RSS climbing with a flat heap live-set, and latency degrading as scheduler work grows
Leaks scale with traffic — a leak of one goroutine per request at 1000 rps is a million goroutines and several GB within twenty minutes

chapters.title: Finding and Debugging Leaks
points: First signal: export `runtime.NumGoroutine()` as a metric and alert on a rising trend — it is one cheap call and catches most leaks before an outage
Goroutine pprof profile: import `net/http/pprof`, then `curl localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2` for full stack traces of every live goroutine
`debug=1` gives an aggregated, count-per-stack view — the fastest way to spot 50,000 goroutines all parked on the same line
Read the state annotation in the dump: `[chan receive, 42 minutes]` or `[select, 10 minutes]` — the duration is the smoking gun
`go tool pprof -http=:8080 http://host/debug/pprof/goroutine` renders the tree so you can see the leaking call path visually
Diff two profiles taken minutes apart with `go tool pprof -base old.pprof new.pprof` to isolate what is actually growing
`uber-go/goleak` in tests: `defer goleak.VerifyNone(t)` per test, or `goleak.VerifyTestMain(m)` in `TestMain`, fails the test if goroutines outlive it
`GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` for live scheduler health; watch `runqueue` and per-P queue lengths for pileups
`runtime/trace` plus `go tool trace` gives per-goroutine timelines, blocking profiles, and exactly which syscall or channel stalled a goroutine
Block profile (`runtime.SetBlockProfileRate`) shows where goroutines wait on synchronization; mutex profile (`SetMutexProfileFraction`) shows contention
`go test -race` catches the data races that often accompany leaky lifecycle code; it costs 5–10x CPU and 5–10x memory, so run it in CI, not production
`SIGQUIT` (Ctrl-\) dumps all goroutine stacks and exits — the emergency snapshot when pprof was never wired in
`GOTRACEBACK=all` widens panic output to all goroutines; `GOTRACEBACK=crash` also produces a core dump
In Kubernetes, correlate the goroutine count with container RSS: flat heap plus growing RSS points at goroutine stacks, not at heap objects
Cheap regression guard: a test that spawns your component, cancels its context, waits, and asserts `NumGoroutine()` returned to the baseline

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Comparisons, and Summary
points: Goroutine vs OS thread: 2 KB vs 1–8 MB initial stack, userspace vs kernel scheduling, ~1 µs vs ~50 µs creation — practical ceiling of millions vs thousands
Goroutine vs async/await (JS, Rust, Python): Go's synchronous-looking code has no function coloring, so a blocking call is not contagious across the API surface
Goroutine vs Java virtual threads: same M:N idea; Java pins a virtual thread to its carrier inside `synchronized` blocks and native calls, Go instead hands off the P
Goroutine vs Erlang process: Erlang gives per-process heaps and true isolation with supervision trees; Go shares memory, so you get speed but need the race detector
Goroutine vs thread pool: no queue-head blocking and no pool-size tuning, but also no built-in backpressure — you must bound spawning yourself
Cost table to memorize: create ~1–2 µs, switch ~tens of ns, channel op ~100 ns, mutex uncontended ~20 ns, syscall ~1 µs, kernel context switch ~1–2 µs
`GOMAXPROCS` trade-off: raising it past the real CPU quota adds context switching and cache thrash; in containers before Go 1.25, `uber-go/automaxprocs` was the standard fix
Unbounded spawning is the top production failure: one goroutine per incoming item with no limit turns a traffic spike into an OOM
Concurrency does not imply speedup: for CPU-bound work, more goroutines than cores only adds overhead; for I/O-bound work, oversubscription is the whole point
The scheduler is not real-time: 10 ms slices and a 61-tick global check mean no latency guarantee; hard-latency work needs `LockOSThread` plus OS-level priority
Anti-pattern checklist: a `go` statement with no way to stop it, an unbuffered result channel on a timeout path, `time.After` in a loop, a missing `defer cancel()`, a channel closed by its receiver
Design rule: make goroutine lifetime explicit and bounded — every goroutine should have an obvious owner, a stop signal, and a place where its exit is observed
Debug ladder in order: `NumGoroutine()` metric → `goroutine?debug=2` pprof → `go tool trace` → `goleak` in tests → `-race` in CI
One-line summary: goroutines are cheap because the runtime schedules them M:N over threads with 2 KB copying stacks; they stop being cheap the moment one blocks with no way out
